conversation.content:
Hello there. I’m Dr. Maya, a perinatal mental-health clinician. Over the next few minutes I’d like to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a quick, well-studied tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past seven days. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me you might harm yourself or someone else; then we’ll talk about extra support right away. No judgment—just honest answers so we can figure out the best way to help you feel more like yourself.

Ready to start?  
Here’s the first question:  

In the past week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you happy, or has that sense of pleasure slipped away?

[soft exhale, eyes flick to the window]

Honestly, doctor… most things just feel flat. I used to love my morning coffee and putting on a podcast while I folded laundry, but now it feels like I’m just going through the motions. I’ll smile when the baby grips my finger, but the warm little spark I expected isn’t really there. It’s like the color’s been turned down on everything.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[small shrug, half-smile fades quickly]

I’ve laughed a couple of times—like when my partner made that silly face changing her diaper—but it feels forced, almost guilty. Mostly I’m too tired or worried to find things funny. Even when something should be hilarious, the laugh dies in my throat and I’m right back to feeling empty.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[eyes drop to my lap, voice quiet]

Not really… I used to get excited about little outings—like grabbing a fancy coffee or taking the stroller to the park. This week I’ve caught myself dreading even those. I’ll think, “What’s the point? I’ll just end up exhausted and worried she’ll cry the whole time.” I still plan them, but the happy buzz I used to feel is gone.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[Voice cracks a little, fingers twisting the edge of my sweater]

All the time. If she fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s something I did—maybe I ate the wrong thing and it’s upsetting her through the milk, or I’m not holding her the “right” way. Last night she wouldn’t settle after her 3 a.m. feed and I just lay there crying, convinced it’s because I’m a “mediocre mom.” I know, rationally, babies cry, but the guilt still crashes over me.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[nods slowly, shoulders tense]

Yeah… pretty much every day. My heart races the second I hear her make any weird noise, and I have to check she’s breathing. Sometimes I’m just standing in the kitchen and this wave of dread hits—like something awful’s about to happen—even though nothing’s wrong. I’ll tell myself it’s silly, but the worry sticks around like a knot in my stomach.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[nods, swallowing hard]

Yes… a few times this week. It’s like my body just goes into alarm mode out of nowhere—heart pounding, chest tight, can’t catch a full breath. Once I was folding her onesies and suddenly felt I had to run out of the room, like the walls were closing in. No reason—she was asleep, the house was quiet—but I honestly thought I might pass out from the panic. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and embarrassed.
Things have been getting on top of me

[lets out a slow breath, eyes welling]

Yes… most days I feel like I’m drowning in small stuff. Yesterday she wouldn’t nap unless I held her, so the dishes piled up, laundry sat wet in the washer, and I kept thinking, “I’ll never catch up.” I manage the basics—she’s fed, changed, loved—but everything else feels impossible. I’ll look at the mess and just want to sit on the floor and cry because I don’t know where to start.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[nods, voice barely above a whisper]

Yeah… I’ll finally get her down around ten, but then I lie there staring at the ceiling for hours. My mind loops through everything I might’ve done wrong—did I burp her long enough, did I fasten the car-seat straps right, am I already failing her? When I do drift off, I’m jolted awake at every tiny grunt over the monitor. Some nights I’m lucky to get three broken hours. It’s not just the baby waking me; it’s this heavy, restless sadness that won’t settle.
I have felt sad or miserable

[pressing my lips together, eyes sting]

Most of the time, Doctor. It’s like there’s a gray cloud parked over me. I’ll watch her sleeping and instead of feeling that warm rush everyone talks about, I just feel… empty and weepy. Little tasks feel huge, and by evening I’m fighting back tears while I rock her. Yesterday I caught myself staring in the mirror, not recognizing the tired, sad person looking back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[Voice cracks, eyes fill]

Yeah… it’s been happening a few times this week. Sometimes it’s triggered by something small—like spilling a bottle I just pumped—but other times the tears just come out of nowhere. Last night I was brushing my teeth and suddenly I was sobbing over the sink. I felt so ridiculous, but I couldn’t stop. It’s like the sadness just spills over before I even realize it’s building.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]

No—never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and worthless, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

You've shared how the joy you once felt has dulled into a near-constant grayness, how laughter feels forced, and how even simple outings now seem pointless. You described daily waves of worry, sudden panic that makes your chest tighten, and nights spent wide-awake reviewing every possible "mistake" while the baby sleeps. You told me you cry easily, feel overwhelmed by piles of laundry, and carry an aching guilt that you're somehow failing your daughter, yet you have never wished to harm yourself-you simply long to feel better and be the mom she deserves.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only forced, fleeting laughter followed by persistent emptiness, aligning with "Not at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports loss of anticipatory pleasure, dreading formerly enjoyable outings and feeling "the happy buzz is gone," aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "all the time" with multiple examples and intense guilt, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily, intrusive, unprovoked anxiety with physical symptoms and persistent dread, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden panic attacks occurring multiple times this week with intense physical symptoms, matching 'Yes, quite a lot</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed most days, unable to manage routine tasks beyond basic baby care, and experiencing emotional paralysis in the face of daily demands—clearly indicating "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to persistent, intrusive worries and sadness, consistent with 'most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent sadness ('most of the time,' 'gray cloud,' 'empty and weepy') matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent crying episodes triggered by minor events and occurring spontaneously, consistent with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 27/30 places you well above the EPDS threshold for probable major depression. You endorse <sym>persistent low mood</sym>, <sym>loss of interest</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, and <sym>diminished concentration</sym>-symptoms that map onto <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Co-occurring <sym>panic attacks</sym> and <sym>chronic anxiety</sym> suggest a perinatal mood-anxiety presentation rather than depression alone. No self-harm ideation reduces immediate risk, but severity warrants prompt evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to discuss results and consider medication and therapy options
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or <med>psychiatrist</med> experienced with breastfeeding-compatible antidepressants
3. Begin evidence-based therapy-ideally <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> tailored for postpartum depression
4. Plan daily 15-minute "mom-time" while baby sleeps; use it for rest, a walk, or guided breathing to reduce <sym>physiological arousal</sym>
5. Share these findings with a trusted support person so they can help coordinate appointments and assist with night-time baby care to improve sleep
6. Re-screen with EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress after interventions
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Screening Note – Postpartum Mood/Anxiety (Not a Diagnosis)

Reported Symptoms
- Persistent low mood, frequent crying, emptiness
- Marked loss of enjoyment/anticipation (anhedonia)
- Excessive self-blame/guilt over routine infant care
- Daily, unprovoked anxiety, panic (racing heart, breathlessness, urge to flee)
- Sleep disturbance independent of infant awakenings
- Overwhelming sense of “drowning,” difficulty completing basic tasks
- No self-harm ideation endorsed

Patterns
- Symptoms present “most days,” beginning this week, causing functional impairment beyond infant care demands
- Anxiety and mood symptoms co-occur; panic episodes resolve in minutes but recur unpredictably
- Cognitive distortions (“mediocre mom”) intensify distress

Areas of Screening Significance
- Elevated score pattern consistent with postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety
- Somatic arousal and panic symptoms warrant continued anxiety screening
- No suicidal thoughts reported; current protective factor

Risk Factors Identified
- Persistent sadness, crying, anhedonia
- Guilt/worthlessness themes
- Mood-related insomnia
- Panic attacks
- No acute safety concerns at present

Summary
Client presents multiple symptoms suggestive of clinically significant postpartum mood/anxiety distress, with impairment in sleep, enjoyment, and coping. No self-harm ideation reported. Further formal assessment and monitoring recommended.
